16786.subject: Music
16786.question_text:
Define the following musical elements and explain their roles in a composition:
(i) Pitch
(ii) Dynamics
(iii) Timbre
16786.explanation:
(i) Pitch: The highness or lowness of a sound, determined by the frequency of vibrations. It is fundamental in melody and harmony.
(ii) Dynamics: The volume of music, indicated by terms like piano (soft) or forte (loud). It adds expression and emotional depth.
(iii) Timbre: The tone color or quality of a sound that distinguishes different instruments or voices, even when playing the same pitch and dynamics.

16787.subject: Music
16787.question_text:
Write the following notes in the treble clef:
(i) Middle C
(ii) E above middle C
(iii) G below middle C
Label each note with its letter name and note value (use a quarter note for all).
16787.explanation:
(i) Middle C: A quarter note placed on the first ledger line below the treble staff, labeled C.
(ii) E above middle C: A quarter note on the first line of the treble staff, labeled E.
(iii) G below middle C: A quarter note on the second space below the treble staff, labeled G.

16788.subject: Music
16788.question_text: Which of the following scales has a pattern of whole and half steps as $W-W-H-W-W-W-H$?
16788.explanation: The pattern $W-W-H-W-W-W-H$ corresponds to the major scale, which is a diatonic scale with seven distinct pitches.

16789.subject: Music
16789.question_text:
(i) Define interval in music.
(ii) Identify the interval between C and G, and state its inversion.
(iii) Explain how the inversion of an interval is determined.
16789.explanation:
(i) An interval is the distance between two pitches.
(ii) The interval between C and G is a perfect fifth. Its inversion is a perfect fourth.
(iii) The inversion of an interval is determined by subtracting the interval number from 9 (e.g., 5th inverts to 4th) and changing the quality (major to minor, perfect remains perfect).

16790.subject: Music
16790.question_text:
Write the following triads in root position, first inversion, and second inversion:
(i) C major
(ii) A minor
Label each chord with its inversion name.
16790.explanation:
(i) C major:
Root position: C-E-G
First inversion: E-G-C (6)
Second inversion: G-C-E (6/4)
(ii) A minor:
Root position: A-C-E
First inversion: C-E-A (6)
Second inversion: E-A-C (6/4)

16791.subject: Music
16791.question_text: Which cadence is formed by the chord progression $V-I$ and provides a sense of finality?
16791.explanation: The chord progression $V-I$ forms a perfect cadence, which is the strongest and most conclusive cadence in Western music.

16792.subject: Music
16792.question_text: Describe three characteristic features of African traditional music and explain their significance.
16792.explanation:
(i) Call and Response: A leader sings or plays a phrase, and a group responds. This fosters community participation.
(ii) Polyrhythm: Multiple rhythms played simultaneously, creating complexity and richness.
(iii) Oral Tradition: Music is transmitted orally, preserving cultural heritage and ensuring adaptability.

16793.subject: Music
16793.question_text: Identify two Ghanaian traditional musical instruments and describe their roles in performance.
16793.explanation:
(i) Fontomfrom: A set of drums used in Akan ceremonies to communicate and accompany dances.
(ii) Gye Nyame: A thumb piano (lamellophone) used in storytelling and recreational music, producing melodic and rhythmic patterns.

16794.subject: Music
16794.question_text:
Compose an 8-bar melody in the key of G major for the soprano voice. Include:
(i) A clear phrase structure
(ii) Appropriate use of dynamics
(iii) A cadence at the end
16794.explanation:
A well-composed melody should:
(i) Have balanced phrases (e.g., 4+4 bars).
(ii) Use dynamics like piano and forte for expression.
(iii) End with a perfect cadence (e.g., $D-G$).
Example: A stepwise melody with occasional leaps, ending on the tonic (G).

16795.subject: Music
16795.question_text: Explain two methods for developing aural skills in music students and provide an example for each.
16795.explanation:
(i) Interval Recognition: Train students to identify intervals (e.g., perfect fifth) by singing or playing examples.
(ii) Dictation: Play short melodies or rhythms and have students notate them. Example: Play a 4-bar melody in C major and ask students to write it down.
